Mehmet Ali Ağca (born January 9, 1958) is a Turkish ultranationalist assassin who murdered a left-wing journalist In Turkey in 1979, and later shot and wounded Pope John Paul II on May 13, 1981, after escaping from a Turkish prison.

The reason for the assassination attempt has never been conclusively determined although it is said that the operation was either: 1) commanded by a Bulgarian military attaché in Italy; 2) under the orders of Iran's Ayatollah Khomeiny; 3) a contract hit on orders and payment by the Turkish mafia; or 4) that the Soviet Union's KGB ordered the assassination, because of John Paul II's support for the Solidarity labor movement in Poland.

As the Pope passed through St. Peter's Square, The Vatican in his open air Popemobile, Ağca fired several shots and wounded him, but was grabbed by spectators and Vatican security chief and prevented from finishing the assassination or escaping. Four bullets hit John Paul II, two of them lodging in his lower intestine, the others hitting his left hand and right arm.

After serving 19 years of imprisonment in Italy where he was visited by the Pope and converted to Christianity, he was deported to Turkey, where he served a ten-year sentence. He was released on January 18, 2010. Ağca has described himself as a mercenary with no political orientation, although he is known to have been a member of the Turkish ultra-nationalist Grey Wolves organization.

On December 27, 2014, 33 years after his crime, Ağca showed up at the Vatican to lay white roses on the recently canonized Saint John Paul II's tomb and said he wanted to meet Pope Francis, a request that was denied.
